h1:
Chiang Mai–Lamphun
One Day, There and Back
intro: Lamphun sits just about 29 km from Chiang Mai — under an hour by car or songthaew. It's an easy cross-province trip: leave Chiang Mai in the morning, walk around the old temples, grab a coffee, eat some northern food, and roll back into the city in time for dinner. We've laid the whole day out as a timeline you can just follow.
chips: 🛺 Out and back in a day

blocks.html: A lot of people staying in Chiang Mai want a day trip that doesn't involve a long drive, and Lamphun fits perfectly — it's close, it's small, and one loop around the old town covers almost everything that matters: thousand-year-old temples, the moat and city wall, cafes facing the temple, and local dishes that are hard to find in Chiang Mai. This article plans it as a there-and-back day: leave Chiang Mai around 8am and be back at your place well before evening.

blocks.text: How to get from Chiang Mai to Lamphun

blocks.html: Chiang Mai to Lamphun is about 29 km, either along Route 106 (the old road) or the Route 11 superhighway, roughly 40–50 minutes of driving depending on traffic. There are a few ways to do it — pick based on whether you have your own wheels and how much convenience you want.

items: Blue songthaew (shared truck) on the Chiang Mai–Lamphun route — catch one near Kad Luang (Warorot Market) by the Iron Bridge. It follows Route 106 under the old rubber trees lining the road, runs frequently, and costs around 25–30 THB per trip. It's the cheapest option and has the most character.
Driving / renting your own car — the most flexible. Parking in Lamphun town is easy to find. Take Route 11 to get there fast, then swing back via Route 106 to enjoy the avenue of rubber trees.

Train — there are Chiang Mai–Lamphun services, but there are few of them and the timings don't line up well with a one-day plan. Better suited to people who just want to try a short train ride than those after convenience.
Taxi / ride-hailing app — convenient but a lot pricier. Makes sense if you're coming as a group and splitting the fare.

blocks.title: Which one to pick
blocks.html: If there are two or three of you and no car, the blue songthaew dropping you right in front of Wat Phra That Hariphunchai is the best value. Lamphun town is fully walkable, so you won't need to catch another ride once you're there. On the way back, pick up a songthaew at the same spot to get to Chiang Mai by evening.

blocks.html: This plan suits first-timers in Lamphun. It focuses on the must-sees in the old town, keeps the walking gentle and unhurried, leaves time for a cafe, and gets you back to Chiang Mai by evening.

blocks.label: There and back in a day
blocks.title: Temples + cafes by the temple

items.note: Hop on a blue songthaew at Kad Luang, or drive yourself along Route 106 to enjoy the rubber trees on both sides.
Lamphun's signature temple, over 900 years old. The golden chedi is the main photo spot — pay your respects, look around the old gateways and bell tower, about an hour.
Right across from the temple — just cross the road. See stone Buddha images and inscriptions from the Hariphunchai era and get a feel for the city's history before you carry on.

items.activity: Cafe by the temple, coffee break
items.note: Inthayongyot Road across from the temple has several cafes, such as Temple House Lamphun (open 07:00–19:00, closed Tuesdays). Sit somewhere cool before lunch.
Try khanom jeen nam ngiao, or the longan-braised pork noodles the town is known for. The shops are within walking distance in the old town.
About 1–2 km from the old town. The stepped Ku Kut chedi is a rare piece of old Lamphun architecture — quiet, shady, good for photos.
Small ancient ruins in the middle of the community. Wander along the moat and earthen rampart around the old town, and grab some cotton textiles and sai ua (northern sausage) to take home.

items.activity: Start heading back to Chiang Mai
items.note: Catch a songthaew at the same spot, or drive Route 11 back into the city — you'll arrive before dark.
In time for an easy dinner in town.

blocks.title: About opening hours
blocks.html: Some museums and temples close on Mondays or Tuesdays, or keep set hours, and a number of the cafes by the temple close on Tuesdays. Check the opening day for the spots you've got your heart set on before you go, so you don't make the trip for nothing.

If you've been to Lamphun before or want a deeper trip, this plan leans into the story of the Hariphunchai kingdom and Pa Sang's cotton weaving. Driving yourself is easier here since there are stops outside the town.

blocks.label: There and back in a day
blocks.title: History + Pa Sang cotton

items.note: Pass through Doi Ti; stop for photos of the old yang trees lining both sides of the road.
Start with the founder of Hariphunchai, then head into Wat Chamadevi to see the Ku Kut chedi and understand the city's roots before the rest of the walk.
The heart of the city — the relic temple associated with those born in the Year of the Rooster. Take in the Lanna architecture.
Pick northern food — khanom jeen nam ngiao, or the local pork-blood soup (kao lao lueat moo).

items.activity: Head to Pa Sang for cotton weaving
items.note: Pa Sang district is about 12 km from town — an old cotton-weaving area. Browse the fabric shops and pick up genuine handmade souvenirs from the community.

items.activity: Nong Ngueak weaving village / longan orchard stop
items.note: See the weaving way of life, and if it's longan season (around Jul–Aug) stop at an orchard to taste fresh longan.
Drive Route 11 back into the city, about 50 minutes.
Trip done, in time for dinner.

blocks.text: Lamphun food worth trying during the day

blocks.html: Lamphun has bold local food that's harder to find than in Chiang Mai. Here's a shortlist to work into lunch or as snacks while you walk. Prices are rough ranges and may shift by shop and time of day.

items.name: Khanom jeen nam ngiao
items.blurb: The dish that goes with the town. The orange nam ngiao broth has a mild sourness from kapok flowers, ladled over rice noodles and eaten with crispy pork rind and fresh vegetables. Old-school shops like Khanom Jeen Pa Sai are tucked in a lane behind the former police station in town.

items.name: Longan-braised pork noodles
items.blurb: Made with longan — the town's famous fruit — braised with pork for a naturally sweet, rounded broth. There's a shop not far from Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, and it's a dish you'll really only find around here.

items.name: Pork-blood soup (kao lao lueat moo)
items.blurb: A rich pork-blood soup. The old shop is along the Lamphun–Pa Sang road, good for anyone who likes bold, homestyle flavor. Add tofu or eat it with rice porridge.

items.name: Sai ua (to take home)
items.blurb: Fragrant grilled herb sausage. The well-known makers in Lamphun do it fresh to old recipes — snack on it with sticky rice or buy some to take home.

items.name: Fresh + dried longan
items.blurb: Lamphun is the longan capital of Thailand. In season (around Jul–Aug) there's juicy fresh longan; off-season there's dried longan and longan juice as souvenirs all year round.

items.name: Local sweets
items.blurb: The morning market and town shops have local sweets to try — khao taen (crispy rice cakes), khanom jok, and northern desserts. Cheap and easy to snack on as you walk.

blocks.title: Eat smart
blocks.html: A lot of the local shops sell out before the afternoon — especially the old-school khanom jeen nam ngiao spots. If you've set your sights on a famous place, move lunch up to before noon and you'll be sure to get a seat.

blocks.text: Cafes by the temple for a mid-trip break

blocks.html: One of Lamphun's charms is the cluster of small cafes around Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, all within walking distance of the temple — perfect for ducking out of the sun and taking some photos.

items.name: Temple House Lamphun
items.blurb: A two-floor cafe with modern decor on Inthayongyot Road across from Wat Phra That. The upstairs rotates art shows. Open 07:00–19:00, closed Tuesdays.

items.name: Black to Basic
items.blurb: An airy, loft-style spot near Wat Phra That on Chai Mongkol Road — an easy place to sit with a coffee.

items.name: Yann
items.blurb: A second-floor cafe beside the temple with plenty of specialty options and sweets. Open late morning to evening.

blocks.text: Tips for planning a one-day trip

items: Leave a little early — head out of Chiang Mai around 8am for a full day, and you'll dodge the rush-hour traffic on the way back.
Dress for temples — you'll be visiting several. Wear a sleeved top and trousers or a skirt that covers the knees to be respectful and able to enter anywhere.
Carry cash — many local shops and songthaews take cash; small bills make life easier.
Sun protection — there's a lot of outdoor walking. Bring an umbrella, hat, and water, especially in the hot season.
Leave time for the return — if you're taking a songthaew, check the last service of the day so you don't lose track of time and miss your ride.

faq.q: Is one day enough to visit Lamphun from Chiang Mai?
faq.a: Easily. Lamphun is just about 29 km from Chiang Mai — under an hour by car or songthaew. The town is small, and a single loop of the old town covers Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, Wat Chamadevi, the museum, cafes, and local food, all in one there-and-back day.

faq.q: What's the cheapest way to get from Chiang Mai to Lamphun?
faq.a: Take the blue Chiang Mai–Lamphun songthaew, which you can catch near Kad Luang (Warorot Market). It runs along Route 106, costs around 25–30 THB per trip, leaves frequently, and drops you right in front of Wat Phra That Hariphunchai. It's the cheapest option and has the most character.

faq.q: Where should I go on a one-day trip to Lamphun?
faq.a: The main stops are Wat Phra That Hariphunchai, the Hariphunchai National Museum, Wat Chamadevi (Ku Kut), Ku Chang–Ku Ma, and a walk through the old town along the moat and rampart. With more time, swing by Pa Sang for cotton weaving and sit at a cafe by the temple for a mid-day break.

faq.q: What Lamphun food should I try?
faq.a: Khanom jeen nam ngiao is the town's signature dish, followed by the longan-braised pork noodles, pork-blood soup (kao lao lueat moo), sai ua, and fresh or dried longan as souvenirs. Many local shops sell out before the afternoon, so eat lunch before noon.

faq.q: When's the best time to visit Lamphun?
faq.a: It's fine year-round. The cool weather from November to February is best for walking the temples. If you want fresh longan straight from the orchard, come around July–August, which is the fruiting season.
